newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - French producer Karmitz bucks cinema trends.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - French producer Karmitz bucks cinema trends.

text.p: Maverick Marin Karmitz, the French film producer who champions European and Third World cinema against the U.S. film industry, is yet again bucking the trend.
He opened a new cinema this month in Paris's poorest arrondissement, the 19th, the only of the capital's 20 districts where all movie theatres had closed down.
"It's going to work," said the Romanian-born former rebel of the May 1968 Paris student riots as reports of good ticket sales landed in his office on the opening day.
The 35 million franc ($7 million) investment is risky, and Karmitz confessed to being as tense as when any of the 52 films he has produced, many of them award-winning, hit the screens.

Besides his money, 58-year-old Karmitz puts his heart in his cinema chain, which he named "14 Juillet" (July 14) after the date of the 1789 Revolution, perhaps to illustrate his ongoing rebellion against the domineering trend of blockbuster films that he calls the rich man's cinema.

His cinemas, which have captured 10 percent of the Paris market, show quality films in their original, sub-titled version. There is no certainty that the residents of the neglected, heavily-immigrant 19th district in northeast Paris will go for them.

Karmitz said he fell in love at first sight with the 120-year-old, Belle Epoque-style pavillion housing a canteen for employees of the Paris Canals Authority and decided to turn it into a six-theatre cinema without even bothering to order a market survey.

The result is an elegant glass and concrete building on the bank of a canal, its walls decorated with one-liners from famous films. Its restaurant boasts a wine list chosen by film director Claude Chabrol, who manned the May 68 barricades with Karmitz.
Karmitz opened the first of his 34 screens 12 years ago near Paris's Bastille square, in a popular district that was being taken over by property developpers. "People told me I was crazy," he said.

The cinema prospered against all odds and helped to instil new life in the district. A grateful Karmitz has kept the headquarters of his production and distribution group MK2 in a backyard near Bastille, well away from rival companies in the chic Champs Elysees district.
Karmitz is fighting the growing, U.S.-inspired trend of taking cinemas to suburban shopping malls, which he says break down the social fabric and turn town centres into deserts.
"A cinema must be like a local cafe, a cinema is life," said the soft-spoken, white-haired former film director.

Karmitz, who backed European Union moves to keep the audio-visual industry out of the GATT world trade pact, said big suburban cinemas also boosted the U.S. film industry, the only one producing enough popular films to keep feeding the screens, at the expense of its ailing European competitor.
He said the European film industry, unable to play to large audiences on the U.S. market because of language differences, was moribund, with the exception of the French industry.

Forty percent of films shown in Paris in the first half of this year were French, against 32 percent from the United States and 17 percent from other European countries. Sixty-four percent of films playing in the 14 Juillet chain were European.
"The world is going to be divided between the rich man's and the poor man's cinema," Karmitz said.
The fight was between filmmakers who master technology and can afford costly special effects and virtual images, and those who, for lack of funds, must keep inventing stories.
"They will substitute imagination for money. This is what I want to fight for because that is how cinema will survive," he said.
Karmitz has produced such award-winning successes as Louis Malle's "Farewell Children", and the late Krysztof Kielsowski's "Three Colours" trilogy of Blue, Red and White.
A resolute foe of violence on the screen, he said films like U.S. director Quentin Tarantino's 1995 Cannes Golden Palm winner "Pulp Fiction" showed absolute contempt for the human body.
"People laugh as they blow up brains, without facing any punishment. This is intolerable," he said.
He refused to distribute Pulp Fiction although he knew that it would be a box office hit.
"I did it knowingly. This is my freedom," he said.
Karmitz said he was aware that he was treading a fine line and refusing to show films could be akin to censorship, but "I am not selling washing powder, I have a responsibility.
"I have fought all forms of censorship, but that does not mean I cannot have rigorous moral standards. I can afford to do what I want. I am independent. This is my own money," he said.
"We are living through barbarian times. I am not sure that I will see the end of the tunnel, but I hope my children will."

His latest project, unveiled this month, is a "City of Image and Sound", a communication complex to open within two years alongside Paris's giant new library, the last of the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand's architectural works.
Karmitz's project will comprise more 14 Juillet screens, studios for three new television channels dedicated to knowledge, health and justice, and halls for debates.
"People feel a real need to speak up," he said. "Their speech has been confiscated by politicians who speak in their name."
